Procedural/applied domains (CS_Eng) show weaker effect. Non-STEM domains require richer models (multidimensional IRT or domain-specific covariates) — reported as acknowledged limitation and future work.\\n   **Paper claim scope**: Domain heterogeneity is established via (a) Simpson's paradox (aggregate ≈ 0, domain-level ≠ 0), (b) STEM gradient with good model fit (3/8 domains with PPP∈[0.1,0.9]), (c) non-STEM misfit as structural boundary of 2PL+γ. Grounded in educational measurement's item compromise IRT (Eckerly 2017, Sinharay 2017) and explanatory IRT (De Boeck & Wilson 2004).\\\\n\\\\n## Core Claims (4 条 — D039 reorder: characterization first, calibration demoted)\\\\n\\\\n1. **Characterization Claim (PRIMARY — D108/D115: domain heterogeneity confirmed at N=24)**: Contamination effects exhibit domain-level heterogeneity within benchmarks, are benchmark-dependent across benchmarks, and scale-dependent. Within MMLU, stratification by cognitive domain (57 subjects → 8 domains) reveals Simpson's paradox: aggregate γ≈0 masks a clear STEM gradient. **N=24 confirmed results (D115)**:\\\\n   - STEM_Math: γ=+0.969, CI excludes 0, PPP=0.438 ✓ (strong positive — contamination inflates factual recall)\\\\n   - STEM_Science: γ=+0.838, CI excludes 0, PPP=0.807 ✓ (strong positive)\\\\n   - STEM_CS_Eng: γ=+0.197, CI includes 0, PPP=0.892 ✓ (null — procedural/applied knowledge less affected)\\\\n   - Non-STEM (Medical, Humanities, Social_Sciences, Business_Law): all PPP≈1.0 → 2PL+γ model structurally misspecified. Negative γ estimates (-0.17 to -0.50) reflect model assumption failure, not true contamination direction.\\\\n   - \\\\\\\"Other\\\\\\\" domain: system crash (disk/cgroup), non-essential catch-all category.\\\\n   **Interpretation**: Contamination susceptibility maps to factual knowledge density — domains rich in memorizable facts (Math, Science) show large positive γ (SFT exposure → recall boost → inflated scores). Procedural/applied domains (CS_Eng) show weaker effect. Non-STEM domains require richer models (multidimensional IRT or domain-specific covariates) — reported as acknowledged limitation and future work.\\\\n   **Paper claim scope**: Domain heterogeneity is established via (a) Simpson's paradox (aggregate ≈ 0, domain-level ≠ 0), (b) STEM gradient with good model fit (3/8 domains with PPP∈[0.1,0.9]), (c) non-STEM misfit as structural boundary of 2PL+γ. Claims based on domains with acceptable PPP ONLY. Across benchmarks: ARC forgetting (γ < 0, CI excludes zero, 3 independent evidence chains) vs GSM8K inflation (γ > 0). Effects are scale-modulated: catastrophic at 0.5B (-17pp ARC), mild at 3B, negligible at 7B. This challenges the dominant \\\\\\\"contamination = uniform inflation\\\\\\\" narrative. Cross-family consistency validated via controlled SFT on 4 independent families (Qwen2.5, Phi-4, OLMo-2, Gemma-2; D141) tests whether contamination susceptibility is a benchmark × domain property, not a model family artifact.\\\\n   **PPP presentation strategy**: Non-STEM PPP=1.0 is not a failure of the analysis but a meaningful boundary finding: 2PL+γ (additive contamination effect on unidimensional ability) captures STEM domain mechanics but not non-STEM. Discuss connection to multidimensional IRT (Reckase 2009) and DIF literature (Holland & Wainer 1993). Consider limited-information fit indices (M2*, RMSEA2) as robustness check for STEM results.\\\\n\\\\n2. **Signal Failure Claim (CO-PRIMARY, headline finding per D039 dream 三档一致)**: Min-K++ exhibits directional reversal at small model scales (Cohen's d = -1.2 to -2.7 at 0.5B d100) — actively misleading, not merely ineffective. S1 embedding similarity is the only reliable signal (AUC>0.95). Multi-signal RRF degrades to S1-only in practice — paper is transparent about this (D039: all 3 dream tiers require honesty here). Training-free RRF remains the principled aggregation design (meta-circularity argument). Must distinguish item-level detection AUC from model-level Cohen's d.\\\\n   **C2 contingency**: \\\\\\\"Scale-dependent\\\\\\\" unverified beyond 0.5B. If 1.5B/3B S2/S4 remain ineffective → downgrade to \\\\\\\"method-specific signal effectiveness.\\\\\\\" Min-K++ reversal remains novel regardless.\\\\n\\\\n3. **Identifiability Claim**: Fisher Information analysis + simulation sweep (20 conditions, 200 runs). Recovery succeeds down to AUC=0.55 (lowest tested) at N≥50; the lower bound remains open. LLM evaluation inherently operates below N≥50 (typically N=8-30), creating a structural domain-method mismatch — this is the real \\\\\\\"impossibility,\\\\\\\" not merely \\\\\\\"IRT needs more data.\\\\\\\" CI width ∝ N^{-0.48} (simulation). Coverage collapse at N<30 confirmed empirically (D036). D039 dream worst-tier caution: frame as domain mismatch insight, not as surprising impossibility.\\\\n\\\\n4. **Conditional Calibration Claim (DEMOTED from old Claim 1 per D039)**: IRT ability estimation provides calibration value (GSM8K: calMAE=0.006 vs raw=0.169, ΔMAE=0.163); the γ parameter provides diagnostic value by revealing domain-differential contamination effects. These are distinct contributions: calibration improvement comes from the IRT framework itself (ability estimation decontaminates via the θ pathway), while γ characterizes where and how contamination manifests. When IRT model complexity matches benchmark structure (2PL for open-ended, 4PL for MCQ) AND signal quality sufficient (validated down to AUC=0.55 at J≥50), calibration produces usable point estimates. Coverage remains below nominal (20-69% at 95%) — present calibrated CIs as directional indicators, not precise credible intervals. Calibration gating criterion: PPP ∈ [0.1, 0.9] AND calibrated MAE < raw MAE. Note: vanilla 2PL ≈ 2PL+γ in MAE across all three benchmarks — γ does not improve calibration accuracy but provides the diagnostic decomposition that is Claim 1's core contribution.\\\\n\\\\n## Contributions (Hierarchical — D039 rebalanced per Dream 2nd round)\\\\n\\\\n### Core (characterization-led; calibration conditional)\\\\n1. **Domain-dependent contamination characterization** via IRT γ_k: Simpson's paradox within MMLU (aggregate γ≈0 masks STEM gradient: Math +0.97 > Science +0.84 >> CS_Eng ≈0), scale modulation, three-regime taxonomy (forgetting / selective memorization / near-immunity). γ heterogeneity maps to factual knowledge density. Non-STEM model misfit as boundary finding (2PL+γ scope limitation)\\\\n2. **Signal failure characterization**: Min-K++ directional reversal (Cohen's d = -1.2 to -2.7) — paper's most citation-worthy empirical finding (D025 + D039 dream 三档一致). Systematic signal × scale × dosage AUC mapping. Honest reporting that RRF = S1-only in practice\\\\n3. **Fisher Information identifiability analysis**: structural vs practical thresholds with domain-method mismatch insight. Strongest theoretical contribution (D025 + D039 一致)\\\\n\\\\n### Supporting\\\\n4. ContamCal framework: two-stage pipeline (S1 provenance → contamination-augmented IRT with per-benchmark γ_k). Conditional calibration with gating criterion. ME model as ablation\\\\n5. Dual-track validation + 7 baselines + 6 metrics (incl. SBC). Controlled SFT injection (internal) + ecological RL (external)\\\\n\\\\n## Story Spine\\\\n- **Problem**: Benchmark scores are increasingly unreliable due to training data contamination. Rephrased test items inflate MMLU accuracy by 8-15 points while evading n-gram decontamination. RL post-training may further complicate detection (under investigation, exp-009). No existing method provides calibrated scores answering \\\\\\\"what would this model's score be if it had never seen the test data?\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**: Detection methods (Min-K%++, ConStat, Self-Critique, KDS) flag contamination but don't calibrate scores. IRT methods (PSN-IRT, Growing Pains, ATLAS, Lalor et al. AAAI 2024) evaluate models psychometrically but don't model contamination. DCR provides adjusted accuracy but lacks uncertainty bounds and RL handling. HiBayES provides Bayesian uncertainty but ignores contamination. Emperor's New Clothes (ICML 2025) demonstrates that all 20 mitigation strategies fail — motivating post-hoc calibration. Dynamic benchmarks (LiveBench) offer an alternative but require continuous curation.\\\\n- **Our framing (D039 pivot, updated D141)**: ContamCal is a diagnostic framework that uses IRT to systematically characterize how contamination affects benchmark scores. Through controlled SFT injection across 4 independent model families (0.5B-14.7B), we reveal the structure of contamination effects — they are bidirectional, scale-dependent, benchmark-specific, and consistent across architectures — and establish the conditions under which statistical calibration is and isn't feasible. Grounded in educational measurement's item compromise IRT (Eckerly 2017, Sinharay 2017) and explanatory IRT (De Boeck & Wilson 2004), with 3 structural adaptations: (a) independent examinees → single model with joint item distribution, (b) binary leakage → continuous exposure scores, (c) stable ability → regime-conditional ability.\\\\n- **Headline result template (D039 — characterization-led, updated D141)**: \\\\\\\"Contamination effects are benchmark-dependent: IRT γ captures forgetting on ARC (γ={X}, CI excludes zero) and inflation on GSM8K (γ={Y}), with scale modulation from catastrophic (-{Z}pp at 0.5B) to {description at 7B-14B} across 4 independent model families (Qwen2.5, Phi-4, OLMo-2, Gemma-2). Detection signal Min-K++ actively reverses direction at small scales (Cohen's d = {W}), making single-signal contamination detection unreliable. Fisher Information analysis establishes that reliable γ recovery requires N≥50 models; recovery succeeded down to AUC=0.55 (lowest tested), with the lower bound remaining open — conditions rarely met in current LLM evaluation.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n## Venue Fit Risks\\\\n- **EMNLP (primary)**: Best venue fit — special theme explicitly invites contamination/data governance. Reviewers deeply familiar with NLP contamination literature (advantage: no need to motivate the problem heavily). Risk: reviewers may be less familiar with IRT/psychometric methods (mitigation: add intuitive explanations, visual pipeline overview, and connection to familiar NLP concepts like calibration/confidence estimation). ~~Risk: may expect broader model coverage beyond Qwen2.5~~ — **Resolved by D141**: 4 independent families (Qwen2.5, Phi-4, OLMo-2, Gemma-2) with controlled SFT at ≤14.7B scale.\\\\n- **AAAI/ICLR (fallback)**: Strong fit for Bayesian/probabilistic methods. Reviewers may need more contamination context but appreciate methodological rigor.\\\\n- **Novelty positioning**: Core method is cross-disciplinary synthesis (detection signals + explanatory IRT + measurement error). NOT positioned as \\\\\\\"new algorithm\\\\\\\" — positioned as (a) signal effectiveness characterization as empirically novel finding, (b) identifiability bounds with theoretical grounding, (c) first framework bridging detection → calibration with proper UQ. RRF is a principled design choice (meta-circularity argument), not claimed as methodological contribution.\\\\n- **RL limitation**: RL models get wide CIs. This is honest — frame as \\\\\\\"calibration is only as good as its inputs.\\\\\\\" Expected regret quantification uses held-out clean benchmark as ground truth (NOT calibrated scores, to avoid circularity).\\\\n\\\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Defenses\\\\n\\\\n| # | Concern | Defense | Experiment |\\\\n|---|---------|---------|------------|\\\\n| 1 | θ and γ identifiable? | Fisher Information analysis + 20-condition simulation sweep (200 runs) + MVP validation | exp-004 |\\\\n| 2 | Why not learned aggregation? | Meta-circularity: learned aggregator's training data may itself be contaminated; RRF is design choice, not contribution | exp-003 |\\\\n| 3 | SFT injection ≠ real contamination | Dual-track: controlled SFT (internal) + ecological RL (external) + near-zero γ check (specificity). SFT is \\\\\\\"best-available proxy\\\\\\\", acknowledged as limitation | exp-006, exp-009 |\\\\n| 4 | Scale limited to 3B | ≤14.7B controlled SFT across 4 independent families (Qwen2.5 0.5B-14B, Phi-4 14.7B, OLMo-2 7B, Gemma-2 9B; D141). 29 runs total. | D141 scope expansion |\\\\n| 5 | Why 4PL not 2PL? | MVP: 2PL γ=0.16 vs 4PL γ=0.34 at N=100; c/d necessary for realistic item modeling | exp-006 |\\\\n| 6 | Too few models (N≈15)? | D025 multi-seed strategy: 3 scales × 4+ dosages × 2-3 seeds = 24-36 models pooled. Target N≥30 minimum (N≥50 ideal). Simulation sweep (exp-004) establishes identifiability at actual N. Growing Pains pre-estimation as backup at very low N | exp-004, exp-001 |\\\\n| 7 | Noisy exposure scores | Measurement error model (exposure as noisy observation of latent τ) propagates uncertainty into posteriors automatically | exp-005 |\\\\n| 8 | No baselines | 7 baselines including DCR (EMNLP 2025) + bootstrap CIs on all comparisons | exp-006 |\\\\n| 9 | Single global γ misspecified? | Per-benchmark γ_k is primary (natural in per-benchmark fitting); joint model with shared global γ is ablation. Report both to show contamination effect heterogeneity across benchmarks | exp-006 |\\\\n| 10 | Local independence violated? | Discussed explicitly; single model responds to all items → item responses correlated through shared parameters. Empirically test via posterior predictive checks on item-level residual correlations. This is a known IRT limitation when N_examinees is small. | exp-006 |\\\\n| 11 | Single model family? | Addressed in main experiments: 4 independent families (Qwen2.5, Phi-4, OLMo-2, Gemma-2) with controlled SFT injection at identical LoRA config (D141). Qwen2.5 provides within-family scaling (0.5B-14B); 3 cross-family models validate generalizability. | D141 scope expansion |\\\\n| 12 | RL regret circular? | Ground truth for regret = held-out clean benchmark scores, NOT calibrated scores. Explicitly stated | exp-009 |\\\\n| 13 | S2/S4 fail at 0.5B — RRF is just S1? | Scale-dependent: honestly report single-signal regime at 0.5B. Verify S2/S4 at 1.5B/3B. RRF value = principled aggregation when signals ARE available + graceful degradation when not. | exp-008, exp-002 |\\\\n| 14 | d100 AUC=0.5 as signal failure? | Labeling artifact: d100 contaminates ALL items → labels lose discriminative power. Must NOT be interpreted as signal degradation. Present only d005/d025 for signal evaluation. | exp-008 |\\\\n| 15 | Novelty ceiling — standard IRT synthesis? (D025, all 3 Dream tiers) | Positioned as cross-disciplinary synthesis, NOT new algorithm. Emergent value: (a) per-benchmark γ_k heterogeneity as benchmark property, (b) Min-K++ reversal as cautionary finding, (c) Fisher Info identifiability boundaries. If 4PL vs 2PL gap small → acknowledge honestly but argue c/d params needed for realistic MC modeling. Report oracle-γ ablation to decompose MAE. | exp-006 |\\\\n| 16 | Per-benchmark γ_k via separate fits, not hierarchical? (D025, [M][W]) | Per-benchmark separate fits = primary (natural, avoids cross-benchmark correlation). Hierarchical γ_k ~ Normal(μ_γ, σ_γ) as ablation to formally test heterogeneity and share info across benchmarks. Both reported. | exp-006 |\\\\n| 17 | Coverage gap — 85% vs 95% nominal? (D025, all 3 tiers) | SBC diagnostic to identify source. Possible causes: local independence violation, insufficient N, model misspecification. Report SBC alongside posterior predictive checks. If gap is from local independence → discuss as known IRT limitation with references. | exp-004, exp-006 |\\\\n| 18 | Why not just S1 alone? (D025, [M][W]) | S1-only is a baseline (#2 single-signal 2PL+γ). If RRF ≤ S1-only → present as \\\\\\\"S1+IRT calibration with extensible multi-signal architecture for future signals.\\\\\\\" Meta-circularity argument for training-free aggregation still holds. | exp-003 |\\\\n| 19 | Coverage collapse 20-33% even with oracle? (D036) | Far worse than #17 anticipated. PPP extremes (ARC=1.0, GSM8K=0.0) = systematic misspecification. Path: (a) increase N via multi-seed pooling, (b) check exp-004 sweep coverage at matching N, (c) if additive γ insufficient → item-level heterogeneity or hierarchical structure. Fallback: lead with MAE+ranking, present coverage honestly. | exp-006, exp-004 |\\\\n| 20 | γ doesn't improve calibration MAE over vanilla 2PL | γ's role is diagnostic (domain-differential characterization), not calibration accuracy improvement. Need: (a) SFT-on-random-data control at 0.5B to isolate capacity vs contamination, (b) focus on 1.5B/3B where capacity effects are minimal (<2pp). Acknowledge 0.5B forgetting as combined SFT+contamination effect. | exp-001 |\\\\n| 23 | N=8/16 contradicts paper's own N≥50 recommendation (D039, all 3 tiers) | Internal contradiction. Path: (a) add N=8 condition to simulation sweep for calibrated expectations, (b) increase N via multi-seed (target N≥30), (c) if N<30 → explicitly position as preliminary with caveats. SBC diagnostic at actual N to decompose coverage gap. | exp-004, exp-006 |\\\\n\\\\n## Evaluation Protocol (6 Metrics — D025 added SBC)\\\\n1. **Calibration error**: MAE between calibrated score and ground-truth clean accuracy, with bootstrap 95% CIs\\\\n2. **Interval coverage**: Fraction of true values within 50%/80%/95% credible intervals\\\\n3. **Interval sharpness**: Average CI width (tighter is better at fixed coverage)\\\\n4. **Ranking preservation**: Kendall's τ between calibrated and ground-truth model rankings\\\\n5. **Dose-response monotonicity**: γ effect increases monotonically with contamination dosage\\\\n6. **SBC diagnostic** (D025): Simulation-Based Calibration (Talts et al. 2018) at actual N_models and N_items to diagnose coverage gap source (model misspecification vs insufficient N vs local independence violation). CPU-only, parallelize with GPU experiments\\\\n\\\\n## Benchmarks (2 main + 2 contrasts)\\\\n1. **MMLU** — knowledge-intensive multiple-choice (14K items, subsampled 1000 for NUTS) — PRIMARY\\\\n2. **ARC-Challenge** — science reasoning multiple-choice (~1.2K items) — PRIMARY. ⚠️ D036: gamma consistently negative (forgetting, not inflation). 3 independent evidence chains: s42 raw (-17.5pp), s123 raw (-10.2pp), oracle IRT (γ=-2.83). Scale-dependent: 3B d100 ARC=84% (mild forgetting) vs 0.5B d100 ARC=29-37% (catastrophic). Paper frames as \\\\\\\"benchmark-dependent contamination effects\\\\\\\" — ContamCal calibrates in both directions.\\\\n3. **GSM8K** — mathematical reasoning free-form (~1.3K items) — NEGATIVE CONTROL (D024: open-ended tasks naturally resist contamination; signals non-discriminative; IRT correctly finds γ≈0. Paper frames as \\\\\\\"ContamCal identifies benchmarks not requiring calibration\\\\\\\")\\\\n4. **HumanEval** (appendix only) — code generation (N=164). Demoted D009: paraphrase QC 16%.\\\\n\\\\n## Baselines (7)\\\\n0. **Raw (no adjustment)** — report original benchmark scores as anchor\\\\n1. **Remove-and-rescore** — drop flagged items, rescore on remaining\\\\n2. **Single-signal 2PL+γ** — best single detection signal + simpler IRT\\\\n3. **Vanilla 4PL** — standard IRT without contamination covariate (γ=0)\\\\n4. **Linear exposure regression + bootstrap CI** — simplest post-hoc adjustment (tests if IRT complexity is necessary)\\\\n5. **Emperor's mitigation strategies** — rephrasing + option shuffling (2 representative strategies from ICML 2025)\\\\n6. **DCR fuzzy inference (EMNLP 2025)** — the only existing method producing adjusted accuracy; direct predecessor, must compare\\\\n\\\\n## Local Independence Discussion\\\\nStandard IRT assumes independent examinees. In LLM evaluation, a single model produces all item responses — responses are correlated through shared model parameters. This fundamentally alters local independence. Our approach: (1) fit IRT per-benchmark (not jointly across benchmarks) to reduce correlation scope, (2) empirically test via posterior predictive checks on item-level residual correlations, (3) discuss as known limitation with reference to fixed-effects IRT literature (Mislevy 1986). The coverage gap (if observed) may partly reflect this violation — measurement error model for exposure partially compensates by widening CIs.\\\\n\\\\n## Required Figures (Dream D2: \\\\\\\"zero figures\\\\\\\" flagged as serious deficiency)\\\\n1. Pipeline overview diagram (2-stage: RRF → 4PL+γ IRT)\\\\n2. Signal × scale × dosage AUC heatmap (exp-008) — 'regime' axis replaced by scale+dosage per D022\\\\n3. Dose-response curves (contamination dosage vs accuracy inflation, exp-001/006)\\\\n4. Identifiability phase diagram (AUC × N_models → γ recoverability, exp-004)\\\\n5. Calibrated-vs-true accuracy scatter with CIs (exp-006)\\\\n\\\\n## Citation Requirements (35+ minimum, expanded per Dream D2)\\\\nMust include: Eckerly 2017, Sinharay 2017, De Boeck & Wilson 2004, Adams et al. 1997, San Martín et al. 2009, Maris & Bechger 2009, Cormack et al. 2009 (RRF), Mislevy 1986, Lalor et al. AAAI 2024, LiveBench, TinyBenchmarks (Polo et al. 2024), KDS, CDD, contamination surveys, SBC (Talts et al. 2018), HiBayES, plus all signals/methods cited in IDEA_BRIEF.\\\\nDream D2 additions (all 3 tiers flagged):\\\\n- DIF literature: Holland & Wainer 1993, Thissen et al. 1993, Zumbo 1999 (γ_k is essentially DIF between exposure groups)\\\\n- ML calibration: Guo et al. 2017, Platt 1999 (disambiguate \\\\\\\"calibration\\\\\\\" — ours is decontamination, not probability calibration)\\\\n- Conformal prediction: Angelopoulos & Bates 2023 (alternative UQ with distribution-free coverage guarantees; discuss why Bayesian IRT preferred)\\\\n- Data attribution: Pruthi et al. 2020 (TracIn), Park et al. 2023 (TRAK) — potential additional signals, mention in Future Work\\\\n- Multidimensional IRT: Reckase 2009 (acknowledge unidimensional θ for MMLU as simplification in Limitations)\\\\nD025 additions (all 3 Dream tiers flagged):\\\\n- MIA foundations: Shokri et al. 2017 (membership inference attacks), Carlini et al. 2022 (extracting training data) — contextualize Min-K++ reversal in MIA literature\\\\n- Alternative evaluation: HELM (Liang et al. 2023), Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al. 2023) — discuss in Related Work as contamination-bypassing alternatives\\\\n- Deeper DCR engagement: Oren et al. 2024 structural comparison\\\\n- Burnell et al. 2023: multidimensional IRT for LLMs (relevant to unidimensional θ limitation)\\\\n\\\\n## Discussion Notes\\\\n\\\\n### D045: 0.5B Position Bias and MC Benchmark Exclusion (2026-05-15)\\\\n- **Finding**: Qwen2.5-0.5B exhibits severe position bias in logprob-based MC evaluation. MMLU prediction distribution: d000 A=46% → d100 A=98%. SFT contamination amplifies pre-existing position prior rather than encoding knowledge.\\\\n- **Decision**: Exclude 0.5B MMLU/ARC data from IRT pooling. Retain 0.5B GSM8K/HumanEval (free-form, unaffected). 1.5B/3B all benchmarks normal.\\\\n- **Paper treatment**: Report in Discussion as \\\\\\\"capacity threshold for reliable MC evaluation.\\\\\\\" The 0.5B dosage-accuracy decline (40→23% MMLU) is position bias amplification, not knowledge degradation. This reinforces Concern #22 (SFT capacity artifact) and motivates the 1.5B+ focus in main results.\\\\n- **Broader implication**: Logprob-based MC evaluation at small scales may be unreliable across model families — note as limitation and suggest token-level or generation-based alternatives for sub-1B models.\\\\n\\\\n## Scope Expansion: ≤14.7B + 4 Families (D141, 2026-05-18)\\\\n\\\\n### Model Matrix\\\\n| Family | Model | Params | Released | Runs | Role |\\\\n|--------|-------|--------|----------|------|------|\\\\n| Qwen (primary) | Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B | 0.5-3B | 2024-09 | existing | Within-family baseline (≤3B) |\\\\n| Qwen (primary) | Qwen2.5-7B | 7B | 2024-09 | 10 (5d×2s) | Within-family scale extension |\\\\n| Qwen (primary) | Qwen2.5-14B | 14B | 2024-09 | 5 (5d×1s) | Within-family scale frontier |\\\\n| Microsoft | Phi-4 | 14.7B | 2024-12 | 5 (5d×1s) | Cross-family, strongest 14B |\\\\n| Allen AI | OLMo-2-7B | 7B | 2024-11 | 5 (5d×1s) | Cross-family, fully open |\\\\n| Google | Gemma-2-9B | 9B | 2024-06 | 5 (5d×1s) | Cross-family, Google family |\\\\n\\\\nAll: bf16 LoRA r=16 α=32 lr=5e-5 (D140: matching ≤3B). 必要性\\\\n\\\\n**框架 3: Qwen-14B specificity（如果 cross-family 14B 不复现 ~2pp）**\\\\n\\\\\\\"The ~2pp MMLU effect at Qwen2.5-14B may be Qwen-specific pre-training artifact, not general contamination case（线性模型无法捕捉）。\\\\n\\\\n### Secondary Findings（Reviewer 评估，2026-05-18）\\\\n\\\\n**高价值（主动追踪）**:\\\\n1. **Cross-family dosage-response shape consistency**: 各 family 在相同 benchmark 上 d000→d100 ContamCal uses IRT with per-benchmark γ_k to systematically characterize these behaviors and establish identifiability boundaries. Calibration is possible conditionally — when model complexity matches benchmark structure (2PL for open-ended, 4PL for MCQ) and signal quality is sufficient (recovery validated down to AUC=0.55, lowest tested, at J≥50) — but the primary contribution is the characterization framework itself. Grounded in educational measurement's item compromise IRT (Eckerly 2017, Sinharay 2017) and explanatory IRT (De Boeck & Wilson 2004).\\n\\n## Core Claims (4 条 — D039 reorder: characterization first, calibration demoted)\\n\\n1. **Characterization Claim (PRIMARY — D108/D115: domain heterogeneity confirmed at N=24)**: Contamination effects exhibit domain-level heterogeneity within benchmarks, are benchmark-dependent across benchmarks, and scale-dependent. Within MMLU, stratification by cognitive domain (57 subjects → 8 domains) reveals Simpson's paradox: aggregate γ≈0 masks a clear STEM gradient. **N=24 confirmed results (D115)**:\\n   - STEM_Math: γ=+0.969, CI excludes 0, PPP=0.438 ✓ (strong positive — contamination inflates factual recall)\\n   - STEM_Science: γ=+0.838, CI excludes 0, PPP=0.807 ✓ (strong positive)\\n   - STEM_CS_Eng: γ=+0.197, CI includes 0, PPP=0.892 ✓ (null — procedural/applied knowledge less affected)\\n   - Non-STEM (Medical, Humanities, Social_Sciences, Business_Law): all PPP≈1.0 → 2PL+γ model structurally misspecified. 1	\section{Related Work}
```text
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Contamination detection and mitigation.}
5	Membership inference for contamination detection builds on the foundations of training data extraction \citep{carlini_2021_extracting}, membership inference attacks \citep{shokri_2017_mia}, early contamination analyses \citep{magar_2022_contamination}, and task contamination studies \citep{li_2024_task_contamination,xu_2024_leakage}. Current approaches include Min-K\% \citep{shi_2023_minkprob} and Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp} (token-level surprisal), ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat} (accuracy gaps on paraphrased items), CDD/TED \citep{dong_2024_cdd} (completion-based probes), KDS \citep{choi_2025_kds} (kernel divergence), TS-Guessing \citep{deng_2024_tsguessing} (temporal splits), and Time Travel \citep{golchin_2024_time_travel} (guided generation probes). Concurrent with our work, \citet{tao2025detecting} propose an entropy collapse method for RL-trained models. \citet{kocyigit2025impact} show that post-training procedures (RLHF, DPO) degrade detection signal reliability; token-level methods become unreliable on instruction-tuned models. \citet{zhang_2024_gsm1k} construct GSM1K as a parallel test set to quantify GSM8K contamination: performance gaps between original and regenerated items serve as a natural experiment for contamination measurement. Recent surveys \citep{chen2025benchmarking,singh2024evaluation} systematically categorize these approaches. These methods flag contamination but do not produce adjusted scores. On the mitigation side, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty approaches and find that none reliably restores clean performance; inference-time decontamination \citep{yang2024inference} and decontamination via forgetting \citep{zhang2025forget} similarly show limited effectiveness. DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} estimates decontaminated scores via fuzzy inference but produces point estimates without uncertainty quantification or domain-level diagnosis. ContamCal consumes detection signals as inputs and feeds them into a calibration framework that estimates decontaminated ability with credible intervals.
6	
7	\paragraph{IRT for LLM evaluation.}
8	Item Response Theory \citep{lord_1980_irt,hambleton_1991_irt} has gained traction as a principled alternative to raw accuracy in holistic evaluation frameworks \citep{liang_2023_helm}. \citet{lalor_2024_irt_nlp} provide a comprehensive IRT tutorial for NLP; TinyBenchmarks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks} uses IRT-informed item filtering for efficient evaluation; Growing Pains \citep{habba_2025_growing_pains} validates IRT at scale on 400+ models and identifies low-respondent limitations; HiBayES \citep{luettgau_2025_hibayes} adds hierarchical Bayesian inference for credible intervals; ATLAS \citep{li_2024_atlas} applies IRT for adaptive testing. Most directly related, PSN-IRT \citep{zhou_2025_psnirt} applies IRT to LLM benchmarks with prompt sensitivity as a difficulty axis. \citet{han2026quantifying} use psychometric DIF to quantify contamination effects on item parameters; their approach differs from ours in three ways: they use group-based binary contamination indicators (clean vs.\ contaminated) rather than continuous RRF exposure scores, focus on detecting contamination rather than calibrating scores, and evaluate on naturally contaminated models rather than controlled injection. Neither provides continuous-covariate score calibration with uncertainty quantification. ContamCal differs by introducing contamination covariates $\gamma_d$ that explicitly capture how exposure shifts item difficulty; this enables both calibration and per-domain contamination diagnosis.
9	
10	\paragraph{Differential item functioning and explanatory IRT.}
11	ContamCal's $\gamma$ parameter is formally an instance of explanatory DIF \citep{holland_1993_dif,thissen1993dif,camilli_1994_dif}: it models how an item-level covariate (contamination exposure) differentially affects response probability across items. In educational measurement, DIF detects unfairness when items function differently across demographic groups \citep{swaminathan_1990_dif,zumbo1999dif}; in our setting, the ``group'' variable is contamination status and the DIF direction indicates whether exposure inflates or deflates performance. We build on the explanatory IRT tradition \citep{deboeck_2004_explanatory_irt}, which incorporates item and person covariates directly into the response model rather than treating them as post-hoc diagnostics. The item compromise literature \citep{eckerly_2017_item_compromise,sinharay_2017_preknowledge} provides the closest psychometric precedent, models of preknowledge effects on compromised items. Our adaptations for LLM evaluation are: continuous (not binary) exposure scores, domain-level stratification, and counterfactual inference via posterior expectation under zero exposure (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).
12	
13	\paragraph{Calibration disambiguation.}
14	We use ``calibration'' in the psychometric sense: adjusting scores to approximate clean (uncontaminated) performance. This differs from probability calibration \citep{guo_2017_calibration}, where the goal is aligning predicted confidences with empirical frequencies. Our reliability diagrams compare calibrated scores against held-out clean accuracy, not predicted probabilities against observed outcomes.
15
```

```text
1	\section{Experimental Setup}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Controlled SFT Injection}
5	\label{sec:injection}
6	
7	We construct a controlled contamination testbed using Qwen2.5 \citep{qwen2024qwen25} at three scales (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B parameters). For each scale, we fine-tune with Low-Rank Adaptation \citep[LoRA;][]{hu2022lora} ($\alpha=32$, $r=16$, lr$=5\times10^{-5}$) on a general-purpose SFT corpus into which benchmark items are injected at four dosage levels: d000 (0\%, clean control), d005 (5\%), d025 (25\%), and d100 (100\%). Injected items are formatted as instruction-response pairs and pass a quality-control filter that removes ambiguous or malformed entries. Contaminated items augment (not replace) the base SFT corpus; at d100, 16{,}533 benchmark items are added beyond 50{,}000 base examples.
8	
9	Each configuration is trained with two random seeds (s42, s123) for a total of 24 models across $3 \times 4 \times 2$ conditions. This within-family design isolates contamination dosage as the primary experimental variable while controlling for architecture, tokenizer, and pretraining data.
10	
11	We exclude 0.5B models from MMLU and ARC IRT due to answer-position bias that correlates with dosage (A-option rate: 46\% at d000 to 98\% at d100; \S\ref{sec:signal_failure}). Three initial 3B checkpoints trained with inconsistent LoRA hyperparameters were retrained under the unified protocol ($\alpha=32$, lr$=5\times10^{-5}$; Appendix~\ref{sec:exclusion_details}). Our pooled calibration analysis (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) uses $J=16$ respondents for MMLU/ARC (1.5B$\times$8 + 3B$\times$8) and $J=24$ for GSM8K (all scales retained). Domain-level $\gamma$ analysis (Table~\ref{tab:domain_gamma}, \S\ref{sec:domain_differential}) uses $J=13$ (1.5B$\times$8 + 3B$\times$5), as it preceded completion of the 3B retraining. The eight 1.5B d000 models serve as the clean reference anchor in both configurations.
12	
13	\subsection{Cross-Family Analysis}
14	\label{sec:cross_family}
15	
16	To test whether IRT calibration is robust to inclusion of new model families, we fine-tune Llama-3.2-3B \citep{grattafiori2024llama3} under the same protocol (d000, d005, d025, d100) with a single seed ($J=4$ additional models). This analysis is \textbf{exploratory}: the single-seed design provides limited statistical power, and results should be interpreted accordingly.
17	
18	Llama-3.2-3B at d100 on MMLU exhibits catastrophic format collapse (all outputs default to option ``A'', accuracy $=0.34$) and is excluded from IRT fitting. ARC and GSM8K at d100 behave normally; the effective Llama MMLU dosage range is therefore d000 to d025.
19	
20	\subsection{Benchmarks, Domains, and Evaluation}
21	\label{sec:benchmarks}
22	
23	We evaluate on three benchmarks spanning distinct cognitive demands and response formats.
24	
25	\textbf{MMLU} \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}: 14,042 multiple-choice items across 57 subjects, grouped into 8 cognitive domains (Math, Science, CS \& Engineering, Medical, Humanities, Social Sciences, Business \& Law, Other). This stratification reveals within-benchmark heterogeneity that aggregate scoring obscures (\S\ref{sec:results}).
26	
27	\textbf{ARC-Challenge} \citep{clark2018arc}: 1,172 multiple-choice science reasoning items.
28	
29	\textbf{GSM8K} \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k}: 1,319 open-ended math problems whose free-form generation format avoids multiple-choice artifacts.
30	
31	We assess calibration quality with six metrics: (1)~mean absolute error (MAE) between calibrated and ground-truth clean accuracy; (2)~Kendall $\tau$ for rank preservation; (3)~credible interval coverage at 50\%, 80\%, and 95\% levels; (4)~posterior predictive $p$-value (PPP $\in [0.1, 0.9]$ indicates acceptable fit); (5)~$\gamma$ direction: posterior probability $P(\gamma\!<\!0 \mid \text{data})$, which reflects evidence strength for a contamination effect; and (6)~split-$\hat{R}$ convergence ($<1.01$).
32	
33	\subsection{Baselines}
34	\label{sec:baselines}
35	
36	We compare against seven baselines: \textbf{B0-Raw} (no adjustment), \textbf{B1-Remove\&Rescore} (drop flagged items; B1b uses RRF-filtered items), \textbf{B2-Single2PL+$\gamma$} (aggregate $\gamma$ without domain stratification), \textbf{B3-Vanilla2PL} ($\gamma=0$, isolating IRT ability estimation), \textbf{B4-LinearRegression} (residuals on exposure scores), \textbf{B5-Emperor} (mitigation strategies from \citet{sun2025emperor}; B5b uses the best-performing variant), and \textbf{B6-DCR} (our reimplementation following \citealp{xu2025dcr}).
```

```text
1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination is pervasive: trillion-token web crawls routinely ingest benchmark items \citep{oren2024proving}, and practitioners cannot determine how much of a reported score reflects genuine capability versus memorization \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. The community has responded with twenty mitigation strategies \citep{sun2025emperor}, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench}, and dynamic regeneration \citep{dong_2024_cdd}, yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: what is the actual effect size of contamination on aggregate scores? Without this measurement, every mitigation decision is made in the dark. Quantifying the real effect of contamination on scores is therefore a prerequisite for any calibration decision.
4	
5	The literature implicitly assumes that the effect is large. Mitigation papers develop elaborate countermeasures; replacement benchmarks sacrifice comparability with established evaluations; correction methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} apply aggressive adjustments. Yet no study has directly measured the aggregate effect size under controlled conditions with uncertainty quantification. The absence of this measurement leaves the field unable to distinguish settings where contamination genuinely distorts rankings from those where it is detectable but practically harmless.
6	
7	Detection methods such as Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at binary classification. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. \citet{han2026quantifying} apply psychometric DIF to quantify contamination effects on item parameters. Our work differs along three axes: (a)~we construct a controlled testbed with known ground-truth contamination labels, whereas they analyze naturally contaminated models where true contamination status is unknown; (b)~we derive identifiability thresholds ($J \geq 50$, AUC $\geq 0.55$) that provide operational guidelines for when $\gamma$-based diagnosis becomes reliable; and (c)~we characterize signal failure modes, including a directional reversal in Min-K\%++ at the 0.5B scale, that affect detection pipeline design. No existing method provides an end-to-end framework for measuring contamination effect size with uncertainty quantification on existing benchmarks.
8	
9	This paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to investigate this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \citep{cormack_2009_rrf}; this sidesteps the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\gamma_d$. Our experiments yield a surprising null result: under SFT injection at $\leq$3B, contamination shifts aggregate accuracy by only ${\sim}$0.6--0.7 percentage points, smaller than the estimation noise of any correction method (pretraining-phase contamination, which may produce larger effects \citep{schaeffer2026causally}, remains an open question). Raw accuracy is already well-calibrated; neither IRT nor $\gamma$-based correction improves upon it. The $\gamma$ parameter nonetheless provides diagnostic value: it reveals domain-level heterogeneity within a model family (Social Sciences $\gamma_d = -0.63$, posterior $P(\gamma_d\!<\!0) = 99.7\%$), while the decomposition analysis explains \textit{why} aggregate scores remain robust despite item-level contamination.
10	
11	Our contributions are as follows:
12	\begin{enumerate}
13	    \item \textbf{Identifiability analysis with a null testbed result.} Simulation studies establish that reliable $\gamma$ recovery requires $J \geq 50$ at signal AUC $\geq 0.55$ (posterior CI width $\propto J^{-0.48}$), well above current LLM evaluation practice ($J = 8$--$30$). These thresholds delineate when contamination-augmented IRT transitions from exploratory to confirmatory. As a testbed result, SFT injection at $\leq$3B shifts aggregate accuracy by only ${\sim}$0.6--0.7pp, smaller than the estimation noise of any correction method.
14	    \item \textbf{Enabling analysis and practical signal findings.} RRF-guided item filtering is a prerequisite for IRT convergence: single-signal selection compresses exposure variance and causes convergence failure ($\hat{R} = 1.53$, ESS$=$7), while RRF fusion preserves broader distributions necessary for $\gamma$ identifiability ($\Delta\tau = 0.18$ vs.\ size-matched random, $0.27$ vs.\ full 2000-item random). As a standalone practical finding, Min-K\%++ exhibits directional reversal at the 0.5B scale (Cohen's $d = -1.55$ to $-1.98$), where the signal is actively misleading rather than merely ineffective.
15	\end{enumerate}
16	
17	Additionally, within-family domain-level analysis reveals directional heterogeneity (Social Sciences $P(\gamma_d\!<\!0) = 99.7\%$, surviving Bonferroni correction for eight tests), a suggestive finding that requires higher-powered replication with $J \geq 50$ models.
```

```text
I found the Phi-4 technical report for you. Here's what I found:

The Phi-4 Technical Report was published on arXiv on December 12, 2024, with the identifier 2412.08905. 

Researchers at Microsoft Research introduced Phi-4, a 14-billion (B) parameter language model designed to focus on data quality. Despite minimal changes to the phi-3 architecture, phi-4 achieves strong performance relative to its size—especially on reasoning-focused benchmarks—due to improved data, training curriculum, and innovations in the post-training scheme.

Key technical details include: The model was initially pre-trained with a four thousand (K) context length, with capacity extended to 16K during mid-training, and used the tiktoken tokenizer for enhanced multilingual support with a vocabulary size of 100,352. Pretraining involved processing 10 trillion tokens with full attention over 4K contexts, employing a peak learning rate of 0.0003, weight decay of 0.1, and a global batch size of 5760.

You can access the full technical report on arXiv at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08905
```

```text
I found the Gemma 2 technical report from Google DeepMind! Here are the key findings:

## Gemma 2: Improving Open Language Models at a Practical Size

The Gemma 2 report details several technical modifications to the Transformer architecture, such as interleaving local-global attentions and group-query attention, and trains the 2B and 9B models with knowledge distillation instead of next token prediction. The resulting models deliver the best performance for their size, and even offer competitive alternatives to models that are 2-3× bigger.

## Key Features

The report discusses several technical approaches:
- Local Sliding Window and Global Attention
- Logit soft-capping
- Post-norm and pre-norm with RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention

## Performance Results

Gemma 27B ranked higher than Llama 3 70B on Chatbot Arena, Gemma 9B ranked similar as GPT-4-0314, and Gemma 2.6B ranked higher than GPT-3.5-Turbo.

**Available Resources:**
- Direct PDF: https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemma/gemma-2-report.pdf
- arXiv: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.00118

All models are released to the community.
```

```text
OLMo 2 is pretrained in two stages using a curriculum approach, with the first stage covering over 90% of the total pretraining budget using OLMo-Mix-1124, a collection of approximately 3.9 trillion tokens from DCLM, Dolma, Starcoder, and Proof Pile II, with the 13B model trained for 1.2 epochs up to 5T tokens.
```

```json
  "old_string": "\\subsection{Controlled SFT Injection}\n\\label{sec:injection}\n\nWe construct a controlled contamination testbed using Qwen2.5 \\citep{qwen2024qwen25} at three scales (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B parameters). For each scale, we fine-tune with Low-Rank Adaptation \\citep[LoRA;][]{hu2022lora} ($\\alpha=32$, $r=16$, lr$=5\\times10^{-5}$) on a general-purpose SFT corpus into which benchmark items are injected at four dosage levels: d000 (0\\%, clean control), d005 (5\\%), d025 (25\\%), and d100 (100\\%). Injected items are formatted as instruction-response pairs and pass a quality-control filter that removes ambiguous or malformed entries. Contaminated items augment (not replace) the base SFT corpus; at d100, 16{,}533 benchmark items are added beyond 50{,}000 base examples.\n\nEach configuration is trained with two random seeds (s42, s123) for a total of 24 models across $3 \\times 4 \\times 2$ conditions. This within-family design isolates contamination dosage as the primary experimental variable while controlling for architecture, tokenizer, and pretraining data.\n\nWe exclude 0.5B models from MMLU and ARC IRT due to answer-position bias that correlates with dosage (A-option rate: 46\\% at d000 to 98\\% at d100; \\S\\ref{sec:signal_failure}). Three initial 3B checkpoints trained with inconsistent LoRA hyperparameters were retrained under the unified protocol ($\\alpha=32$, lr$=5\\times10^{-5}$; Appendix~\\ref{sec:exclusion_details}). Our pooled calibration analysis (Table~\\ref{tab:baselines}) uses $J=16$ respondents for MMLU/ARC (1.5B$\\times$8 + 3B$\\times$8) and $J=24$ for GSM8K (all scales retained). Domain-level $\\gamma$ analysis (Table~\\ref{tab:domain_gamma}, \\S\\ref{sec:domain_differential}) uses $J=13$ (1.5B$\\times$8 + 3B$\\times$5), as it preceded completion of the 3B retraining. The eight 1.5B d000 models serve as the clean reference anchor in both configurations.\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Family Analysis}\n\\label{sec:cross_family}\n\nTo test whether IRT calibration is robust to inclusion of new model families, we fine-tune Llama-3.2-3B \\citep{grattafiori2024llama3} under the same protocol (d000, d005, d025, d100) with a single seed ($J=4$ additional models). This analysis is \\textbf{exploratory}: the single-seed design provides limited statistical power, and results should be interpreted accordingly.\n\nLlama-3.2-3B at d100 on MMLU exhibits catastrophic format collapse (all outputs default to option ``A'', accuracy $=0.34$) and is excluded from IRT fitting. ARC and GSM8K at d100 behave normally; the effective Llama MMLU dosage range is therefore d000 to d025.",
  "new_string": "\\subsection{Controlled SFT Injection}\n\\label{sec:injection}\n\nWe construct a controlled contamination testbed spanning four independent model families from four labs, trained on independent corpora with distinct pre-training recipes: Qwen2.5 \\citep{qwen2024qwen25} (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B), Phi-4 \\citep{abdin2024phi4} (14.7B), OLMo-2 \\citep{olmo2team2025} (7B), and Gemma-2 \\citep{gemmateam2024gemma2} (9B). All models are fine-tuned with a unified LoRA configuration \\citep{hu2022lora} ($r=16$, $\\alpha=32$, lr$=5\\times10^{-5}$, bf16) on a general-purpose SFT corpus into which benchmark items are injected at five dosage levels: d000 (0\\%, clean control), d005 (5\\%), d025 (25\\%), d050 (50\\%), and d100 (100\\%). Contaminated items augment (not replace) the base SFT corpus; at d100, 16{,}533 benchmark items are added beyond 50{,}000 base examples.\n\nQwen2.5 serves as the primary within-family series, providing five scale points (0.5B--14B) for studying scale-dependent contamination effects. Models at $\\leq$3B are trained with two seeds (s42, s123); 7B and 14B use two and one seed respectively. The three cross-family models (Phi-4, OLMo-2, Gemma-2) are each trained at five dosages with a single seed. This yields 24 within-family checkpoints at $\\leq$3B (existing), 15 additional Qwen models at 7B--14B, and 15 cross-family models, for a total of 54 model checkpoints.\n\nWe exclude 0.5B models from MMLU and ARC IRT due to answer-position bias that correlates with dosage (A-option rate: 46\\% at d000 to 98\\% at d100; \\S\\ref{sec:signal_failure}). Three initial 3B checkpoints trained with inconsistent LoRA hyperparameters were retrained under the unified protocol (Appendix~\\ref{sec:exclusion_details}).\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Family Validation}\n\\label{sec:cross_family}\n\nThe cross-family design tests whether contamination effects generalize beyond a single model family. Phi-4 (14.7B) provides a second data point at the 14B frontier from an independent lab; OLMo-2 (7B) and Gemma-2 (9B) validate at the 7--9B band. Each cross-family model is trained at all five dosage levels with a single seed. This single-seed design provides limited statistical power per family; cross-family results should be interpreted as consistency checks rather than independent confirmatory analyses."
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Introduction}\\label{sec:introduction}\n\nBenchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination is pervasive: trillion-token web crawls routinely ingest benchmark items \\citep{oren2024proving}, and practitioners cannot determine how much of a reported score reflects genuine capability versus memorization \\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. The community has responded with twenty mitigation strategies \\citep{sun2025emperor}, contamination-free benchmarks \\citep{white2024livebench}, and dynamic regeneration \\citep{dong_2024_cdd}, yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: what is the actual effect size of contamination on aggregate scores? Without this measurement, every mitigation decision is made in the dark. Quantifying the real effect of contamination on scores is therefore a prerequisite for any calibration decision.\n\nThe literature implicitly assumes that the effect is large. Mitigation papers develop elaborate countermeasures; replacement benchmarks sacrifice comparability with established evaluations; correction methods like DCR \\citep{xu2025dcr} apply aggressive adjustments. Yet no study has directly measured the aggregate effect size under controlled conditions with uncertainty quantification. The absence of this measurement leaves the field unable to distinguish settings where contamination genuinely distorts rankings from those where it is detectable but practically harmless.\n\nDetection methods such as Min-K\\%++ \\citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \\citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \\citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at binary classification. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \\citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \\citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. \\citet{han2026quantifying} apply psychometric DIF to quantify contamination effects on item parameters. Our work differs along three axes: (a)~we construct a controlled testbed with known ground-truth contamination labels, whereas they analyze naturally contaminated models where true contamination status is unknown; (b)~we derive identifiability thresholds ($J \\geq 50$, AUC $\\geq 0.55$) that provide operational guidelines for when $\\gamma$-based diagnosis becomes reliable; and (c)~we characterize signal failure modes, including a directional reversal in Min-K\\%++ at the 0.5B scale, that affect detection pipeline design. No existing method provides an end-to-end framework for measuring contamination effect size with uncertainty quantification on existing benchmarks.\n\nThis paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to investigate this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \\citep{cormack_2009_rrf}; this sidesteps the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\\gamma_d$. Our experiments yield a surprising null result: under SFT injection at $\\leq$3B, contamination shifts aggregate accuracy by only ${\\sim}$0.6--0.7 percentage points, smaller than the estimation noise of any correction method (pretraining-phase contamination, which may produce larger effects \\citep{schaeffer2026causally}, remains an open question). Raw accuracy is already well-calibrated; neither IRT nor $\\gamma$-based correction improves upon it. The $\\gamma$ parameter nonetheless provides diagnostic value: it reveals domain-level heterogeneity within a model family (Social Sciences $\\gamma_d = -0.63$, posterior $P(\\gamma_d\\!<\\!0) = 99.7\\%$), while the decomposition analysis explains \\textit{why} aggregate scores remain robust despite item-level contamination.\n\nOur contributions are as follows:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{Identifiability analysis with a null testbed result.} Simulation studies establish that reliable $\\gamma$ recovery requires $J \\geq 50$ at signal AUC $\\geq 0.55$ (posterior CI width $\\propto J^{-0.48}$), well above current LLM evaluation practice ($J = 8$--$30$). These thresholds delineate when contamination-augmented IRT transitions from exploratory to confirmatory. As a testbed result, SFT injection at $\\leq$3B shifts aggregate accuracy by only ${\\sim}$0.6--0.7pp, smaller than the estimation noise of any correction method.\n    \\item \\textbf{Enabling analysis and practical signal findings.} RRF-guided item filtering is a prerequisite for IRT convergence: single-signal selection compresses exposure variance and causes convergence failure ($\\hat{R} = 1.53$, ESS$=$7), while RRF fusion preserves broader distributions necessary for $\\gamma$ identifiability ($\\Delta\\tau = 0.18$ vs.\\ size-matched random, $0.27$ vs.\\ full 2000-item random). As a standalone practical finding, Min-K\\%++ exhibits directional reversal at the 0.5B scale (Cohen's $d = -1.55$ to $-1.98$), where the signal is actively misleading rather than merely ineffective.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nAdditionally, within-family domain-level analysis reveals directional heterogeneity (Social Sciences $P(\\gamma_d\\!<\\!0) = 99.7\\%$, surviving Bonferroni correction for eight tests), a suggestive finding that requires higher-powered replication with $J \\geq 50$ models.",
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related_work}\n\n\\paragraph{Contamination detection and mitigation.}\nMembership inference for contamination detection builds on the foundations of training data extraction \\citep{carlini_2021_extracting}, membership inference attacks \\citep{shokri_2017_mia}, early contamination analyses \\citep{magar_2022_contamination}, and task contamination studies \\citep{li_2024_task_contamination,xu_2024_leakage}. Current approaches include Min-K\\% \\citep{shi_2023_minkprob} and Min-K\\%++ \\citep{zhang_2024_minkpp} (token-level surprisal), ConStat \\citep{dekoninck2024constat} (accuracy gaps on paraphrased items), CDD/TED \\citep{dong_2024_cdd} (completion-based probes), KDS \\citep{choi_2025_kds} (kernel divergence), TS-Guessing \\citep{deng_2024_tsguessing} (temporal splits), and Time Travel \\citep{golchin_2024_time_travel} (guided generation probes). Concurrent with our work, \\citet{tao2025detecting} propose an entropy collapse method for RL-trained models. \\citet{kocyigit2025impact} show that post-training procedures (RLHF, DPO) degrade detection signal reliability; token-level methods become unreliable on instruction-tuned models. \\citet{zhang_2024_gsm1k} construct GSM1K as a parallel test set to quantify GSM8K contamination: performance gaps between original and regenerated items serve as a natural experiment for contamination measurement. Recent surveys \\citep{chen2025benchmarking,singh2024evaluation} systematically categorize these approaches. These methods flag contamination but do not produce adjusted scores. On the mitigation side, \\citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty approaches and find that none reliably restores clean performance; inference-time decontamination \\citep{yang2024inference} and decontamination via forgetting \\citep{zhang2025forget} similarly show limited effectiveness. DCR \\citep{xu2025dcr} estimates decontaminated scores via fuzzy inference but produces point estimates without uncertainty quantification or domain-level diagnosis. ContamCal consumes detection signals as inputs and feeds them into a calibration framework that estimates decontaminated ability with credible intervals.\n\n\\paragraph{IRT for LLM evaluation.}\nItem Response Theory \\citep{lord_1980_irt,hambleton_1991_irt} has gained traction as a principled alternative to raw accuracy in holistic evaluation frameworks \\citep{liang_2023_helm}. \\citet{lalor_2024_irt_nlp} provide a comprehensive IRT tutorial for NLP; TinyBenchmarks \\citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks} uses IRT-informed item filtering for efficient evaluation; Growing Pains \\citep{habba_2025_growing_pains} validates IRT at scale on 400+ models and identifies low-respondent limitations; HiBayES \\citep{luettgau_2025_hibayes} adds hierarchical Bayesian inference for credible intervals; ATLAS \\citep{li_2024_atlas} applies IRT for adaptive testing. Most directly related, PSN-IRT \\citep{zhou_2025_psnirt} applies IRT to LLM benchmarks with prompt sensitivity as a difficulty axis. \\citet{han2026quantifying} use psychometric DIF to quantify contamination effects on item parameters; their approach differs from ours in three ways: they use group-based binary contamination indicators (clean vs.\\ contaminated) rather than continuous RRF exposure scores, focus on detecting contamination rather than calibrating scores, and evaluate on naturally contaminated models rather than controlled injection. In educational measurement, DIF detects unfairness when items function differently across demographic groups \\citep{swaminathan_1990_dif,zumbo1999dif}; in our setting, the ``group'' variable is contamination status and the DIF direction indicates whether exposure inflates or deflates performance. We build on the explanatory IRT tradition \\citep{deboeck_2004_explanatory_irt}, which incorporates item and person covariates directly into the response model rather than treating them as post-hoc diagnostics. The item compromise literature \\citep{eckerly_2017_item_compromise,sinharay_2017_preknowledge} provides the closest psychometric precedent, models of preknowledge effects on compromised items. 1	\section*{Limitations}
```
```text
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3

5	
6	\paragraph{Scale ceiling.}
7	All experiments use models at or below 3B parameters. Larger models (7B+) may exhibit qualitatively different contamination dynamics where SFT injection is absorbed without producing measurable signal divergence.

10	S1 (embedding similarity) requires training corpus access, unavailable for closed-source models. For API-only models, only S2 and S4 are applicable, and both show poor discrimination below 1.5B (\S\ref{sec:signal_failure}).
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section*{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nWe identify nine limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.\n\n\\paragraph{Scale ceiling.}\nAll experiments use models at or below 3B parameters. Our domain-level analysis ($J = 13$) yields a strong directional signal (posterior $P(\\gamma<0) > 99\\%$) for only one of eight MMLU domains. Per-domain $\\gamma$ diagnosis at current ensemble sizes is exploratory.\n\n\\paragraph{Position bias.}\nQwen2.5-0.5B exhibits position bias correlated with dosage (A-option rate: 46\\% at d000 to 98\\% at d100); these models are excluded from MC IRT analyses, which reduces ensemble size.\n\n\\paragraph{Credible interval coverage.}\nCI coverage is benchmark-dependent (\\S\\ref{sec:calibration_results}), computed on 18 checkpoints for MMLU and 20 for ARC. 57	\subsection{Identifiability and Value Decomposition}
```
```text
58	\label{sec:fisher}
59	\label{sec:value_decomposition}
60	
61	The reliability of $\gamma$ depends on signal quality (AUC) and ensemble size $J$: Fisher information $\mathcal{I}(\gamma) \propto \text{Var}(e_{\cdot i})$, which collapses when signal AUC is low. Simulation validates that recovery requires AUC$\geq$0.55 with $J \geq 50$ (\S\ref{sec:identifiability}), above current practice ($J = 8$--$30$; \citealp{habba_2025_growing_pains,lalor_2024_irt_nlp,schroeders_2025_irt_sample_size}).
62	
63	Eq.~\eqref{eq:calibrated} depends on $\theta_j$, not $\gamma$ directly: IRT ability estimation separates stable capability from item-level noise regardless of the contamination model. This predicts vanilla 2PL ($\gamma\!=\!0$) achieves comparable calibration to 2PL+$\gamma$, with $\gamma_d$ serving diagnosis rather than calibration (\S\ref{sec:calibration_results}).
```
